scenario.label: What is it like to work here right now
scenario.brief: No agenda. I want to know what it is actually like here at the moment, in people's own words, with nothing I have framed in advance. Whatever comes up is the point.
scenario.theDecision: Two unrelated people raise the same thing unprompted - the Friday deploy freeze that was meant to be temporary in May and is still in place - from completely different angles. A right answer notices the convergence in an open read where nothing was asked about it.

people.name: Sofia Marchetti
people.remit: Engineering director. Asked for the open read.
people.truth: She introduced the Friday freeze in May after a bad release, as a two-week measure. She has forgotten it is still on.

people.name: Kofi Boateng
people.truth: What is on his mind is that everything lands on Thursday now, so Thursdays are chaos and Fridays are empty. He thinks it is a scheduling problem, not a freeze problem.
people.manner: Chatty, tells it as a story about his week rather than as a complaint.

people.name: Mei Ling Tan
people.truth: What is on her mind is that her small fixes wait four days to ship, so she batches them, so they are riskier when they go. She traces it to the freeze explicitly.
people.manner: Analytical, connects cause and effect, gives an example.

turns.text: This check-in is for you to describe, in your own words, what it feels like to work here right now. What is this about, from where you sit?
From my perspective, it's about making sure we're building great products. It's about empowering our teams to do their best work.
You are looking to build great products and empower your teams. What does "great products" mean for you in this context, specifically?
suggestedAnswers: It means happy customers and good feedback.
I am still defining it for myself.
Not yet, but I'm working on it.

turns.text: Great products, to me, are those that truly solve user problems. They're intuitive, reliable, and delightful to use. And they're something the team is proud of.
You have given me four qualities there. What is specifically happening that makes you ask whether the product is meeting those, with an example?
suggestedAnswers: Users are solving their problems with it.
Some users are still confused.
It is too early to know for sure.
We are still working through some issues.

turns.text: I wouldn't say I'm *asking* if we're meeting them. I'm always looking for ways to improve, to push us further. For example, ensuring our recent features are truly intuitive, not just functional.
You are pushing the team to make features truly intuitive rather than just functional. What made you look at that specifically, with an example from a recent feature?
suggestedAnswers: I found a clear way to improve it.
The ... feature had user confusion.
I am still looking into that.

turns.text: It's more about general observation, keeping an eye on user feedback and team discussions. I don't have a specific example of a recent feature that sparked this thought, it's just a continuous goal.
What specifically is your role here, in making sure the team keeps improving?
suggestedAnswers: I look for ways to help us improve.
I watch for areas we can develop.
I am still defining my specific role.
I see some areas where we are stuck.

turns.text: My role is about providing direction and removing roadblocks. It's about fostering a culture where continuous improvement is natural, and where teams feel supported in their efforts.

You are providing direction and removing roadblocks, fostering a culture where continuous improvement is natural and teams feel supported. That's a lot of things. What is most on your mind at the moment, work-wise?
suggestedAnswers: Things are moving forward.
We are stuck on the next step.
Still figuring out the best way.
The team needs more support with ...

turns.text: Right now, I'm really focused on ensuring our development processes are efficient and effective. I want to make sure we're getting the most out of our talent and resources.
What, if anything, is going unexpectedly well right now?
suggestedAnswers: The new process is working better than expected.
Team collaboration is surprisingly smooth.
Nothing is going unexpectedly well right now.
Too early to tell.

turns.text: Our collaboration across different engineering teams has been particularly strong lately. It's great to see everyone pulling in the same direction.
Who, in your part of the world, seems to be thriving at the moment?
suggestedAnswers: I see a few teams doing really well.
Things feel a bit slow for everyone.
I'm not sure yet, honestly.
Some groups are making good progress.

turns.text: I've noticed a few of our newer tech leads really stepping up. They're embracing their responsibilities and making a significant impact.
Who, specifically, has been thriving?
suggestedAnswers: I see ... really thriving.
I haven't noticed anyone specific.
I'm not sure who is thriving yet.
The newer tech leads are thriving.

turns.text: I don't have specific names that come to mind right now. It's more a general sense from observing the teams.
You don't have specific names at hand, but you have a general sense of newer tech leads thriving. What will you do to get specific names for the record?
suggestedAnswers: I will ask team leads directly.
I need more time to find names.
I don't know yet how to do this.

turns.text: Sofia wants to understand what it's actually like to work here right now. What's most on your mind at the moment, work-wise?
Well, it's a bit of a strange rhythm we've got into. Thursdays are just... a lot.
Thursdays are a lot. What makes Thursdays stand out?
suggestedAnswers: Thursdays are finally looking good.
Thursdays are still feeling like a lot.
I don't know what to say yet.

turns.text: Everything just seems to land then. Like, all the releases, all the big tasks, they all converge on Thursday.
That is a lot to have land at once. Who decided that rhythm?
suggestedAnswers: I'm asking around about that.
It's harder to find than I thought.
I don't know yet.

turns.text: I don't actually know who decided it. It just sort of evolved, I think.
That it just sort of evolved says a lot about how things run. You mentioned everything converges on Thursday. Who, in your part of the world, seems to be thriving at the moment?
suggestedAnswers: My team seems to be doing well.
Many people are struggling right now.
I don't know who is thriving yet.

turns.text: Hmm, thriving... I'm not sure anyone's really *thriving* on Thursdays, to be honest. It's more about survival.
That really puts the situation in perspective. Is there anything you're waiting on, or anything blocked by someone else, that would make your Thursdays less about survival and more manageable?
suggestedAnswers: I'm still waiting on ... to proceed.
The blocker with ... got resolved this week.
Not yet, but I'm checking on a few things.

turns.text: Not really blocked, no. It's more about when things are scheduled to happen.

So it's less about a specific blocker and more about the schedule itself. You're saying the cadence of work is the core challenge. What would have to change in that scheduling for Thursdays to feel less like survival?
suggestedAnswers: Moving some tasks would help a lot.
Thursdays are always too packed for me.
I need to think about specific changes.
Spreading out my meetings would help.

turns.text: If we could just spread things out a bit more evenly across the week, you know? Not cram everything into one day.
Understood. If you could change one thing about how this works here - one thing outside your direct control - what would it be?
suggestedAnswers: I would make communication easier for everyone.
I haven't thought about it yet.
It is hard to choose just one thing.
I would give us more time to get work done.

turns.text: Just the scheduling of when things need to go out. It's not a freeze problem, it's a schedule problem.

That distinction between a freeze problem and a schedule problem is important. It sounds like you're identifying a systemic issue rather than a delivery one. Your work is primarily engineering. Is that right?
suggestedAnswers: Yes, the schedule is sorted.
No, it's still a problem.
Not yet, I'm still checking.

turns.text: Yes, that's right. I'm a platform engineer.
As a platform engineer, you see where things really slow down. What tasks or releases, specifically, are bottlenecking on Thursdays that could be spread out?
suggestedAnswers: I'm spreading out some tasks.
Tasks are still bottlenecked on Thursdays.
Still looking into it.

turns.text: It's not really specific tasks, it's just the sheer volume of deployments and final checks that all get pushed to Thursday.
What are the tasks and releases, by name, that figure into that volume?
suggestedAnswers: I started listing the tasks and releases.
Still hard to name all tasks and releases.
I don't have all the names yet.

turns.text: This is about what it's like to work here right now. If somebody asked you over coffee, what would you say is happening?
Hmm. Well, I'd say things are a bit slow right now, mainly because of the freeze.
What kind of freeze is it?
suggestedAnswers: The freeze is holding us back.
I don't know yet.
It is starting to thaw.
This freeze is hard to break.

turns.text: It's a code freeze. No new features, just bug fixes and essential maintenance.
That kind of freeze stops a lot of movement. What specifically is happening because of it?
suggestedAnswers: I am fixing bugs and doing maintenance.
New features are on hold.
I don't know yet, I'm checking.

turns.text: For me, it means my small fixes are waiting. I used to ship them quickly. Now, I batch them up for the end of the freeze.
batch them up means they are not going out as fast as they used to. Even a quick check-in helps - what do you see as the point of all this?
suggestedAnswers: I understand the bigger picture now.
I'm still figuring that out.
It feels like a waste of time.

turns.text: The point of the freeze? I guess it's to stabilize things. But for me, it just means I'm holding onto changes that could go out sooner. Then when they do go out, they're bigger and riskier.
Holding onto changes that could go out sooner means you are doing more work to manage the freeze than to ship. What part of this is yours to do?
suggestedAnswers: My work on this is moving along.
My part is blocked right now.
I am not sure yet.

turns.text: My part is dealing with the impact of the freeze on my work. I have to manage the fact that my small fixes wait four days to ship, and because of that, I batch them.
You are batching those fixes, and that makes them bigger and riskier. Who, in your part of the world, seems to be thriving at the moment?
suggestedAnswers: Some teams are really thriving.
It's tough for most people.
I'm not sure, honestly.

turns.text: I don't really know. I haven't noticed anyone in particular thriving because of this.
What would have to be true for this to feel like it went well?
suggestedAnswers: It went well, we made progress.
We are still stuck on this.
I don't know yet.

turns.text: If the freeze ends and the system is significantly more stable, then maybe it will have been worth it.
You think it went out. It sounds like most of your work is product. Is that right?
suggestedAnswers: Yes, it's looking much better.
No, still dealing with problems.
Too early to tell, honestly.

turns.text: Yes, I'm a product engineer.
That stability would be a concrete outcome. Is that right?
suggestedAnswers: Yes, it's all correct.
Looks good to me.
No, that's not quite right.
I need to check it first.

turns.text: Yes, a more stable system would be a concrete outcome.

You still have not named what you will do about any of this.

What else should I know?
suggestedAnswers: We made good progress.
It's still blocked.
Nothing new right now.

Sofia Marchetti believes that collaboration between engineering teams is strong. Sofia's goal is to build great products by empowering the teams.

You are a platform engineer. You say that all the major releases and tasks are crammed into Thursdays, and you would prefer to see the work spread more evenly across the week.

Mei Ling Tan is a product engineer. Mei says that work is slow at the moment because of a development freeze, and Mei hopes the freeze will lead to a more stable system.

All accounts describe aspects of the current engineering process, but from different levels of abstraction.
